lessons.title: Surface Preparation in African Climates
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 8. This lesson is about the single most important step in any painting or decorating job: surface preparation. In Africa, where we deal with intense sun, heavy rains, high humidity, dust, and uneven substrates, preparation is not optional. It is the difference between a finish that lasts two years and one that lasts ten. As a business owner or technician, your reputation is built on how long your work lasts. Clients will not remember the colour you recommended. They will remember the paint peeling off their wall after one rainy season. So let us treat preparation as a profit centre, not a chore. First, assess the substrate. In many African markets, you will encounter walls made of cement blocks, burnt bricks, mud, stone, or a combination. Each behaves differently. Cement block walls are porous and often have efflorescence, that white powdery deposit caused by salts migrating to the surface. If you paint over efflorescence, the paint will blister and flake. The fix is to dry-brush the salts off, wash with a diluted acid solution or a proprietary efflorescence remover, rinse thoroughly, and allow to dry completely. In coastal cities like Mombasa, Lagos, or Durban, salt-laden air accelerates this problem, so you may need a specialised alkali-resistant primer. Second, check moisture content. A wall can look dry on the surface but hold moisture deep inside. In the rainy season, this is very common. Use a moisture meter if you can afford one, or the simple plastic sheet test: tape a square of clear plastic to the wall, leave it for 24 hours, and check for condensation. If moisture is present, do not paint. Instead, identify the source. Is it rising damp from the foundation? A leaking roof? Poor drainage around the building? Painting over damp is throwing money away. You may need to recommend a damp-proof course, improved ventilation, or exterior drainage before any coating is applied. Third, repair defects. Cracks, holes, and uneven surfaces must be filled. In Africa, we often use cement-based fillers, but these can shrink and crack. For interior work, gypsum-based fillers sand more easily. For exterior work, use a flexible acrylic filler that can move with the wall. Large cracks should be widened into a V-shape, cleaned, primed, and filled in layers rather than one thick application. Allow each layer to dry before the next. This takes time, but it prevents callbacks. Fourth, clean the surface. Dust, grease, mould, and old flaking paint must be removed. In kitchens and industrial areas, grease is a major issue. Use a degreaser and rinse well. Mould is common in humid regions and must be treated with a fungicidal wash. Simply painting over mould means it will return. Scrape off all loose and flaking paint. Sand edges smooth. For previously painted surfaces, check whether the old paint is oil-based or water-based. You can test with a cloth soaked in methylated spirits; if the paint softens, it is water-based. This matters because you cannot apply a water-based paint over a glossy oil-based surface without a bonding primer. Fifth, consider the environment. In dusty areas, you may need to dampen the ground or use screens to prevent dust settling on wet paint. In hot, dry regions, paint dries too fast, leading to brush marks and poor adhesion. You can add a retarder or work in the early morning. In humid regions, paint dries slowly, which can cause sagging and runs. Plan your work around the weather. As a business, you should build a preparation checklist and price it properly. Many painters lose money because they underestimate preparation time. A good rule is that preparation should be 60 to 70 percent of the total job time. If you quote too low, you will either cut corners or lose profit. Instead, educate the client. Explain why preparation costs what it does. Show them photos of failed jobs caused by poor preparation. Offer a warranty that is conditional on proper preparation. This builds trust and justifies your price. Finally, think about tools. You need scrapers, wire brushes, sanding blocks, filling knives, a good quality dust mask, safety goggles, and gloves. In many African markets, these are affordable and available. Do not compromise on safety. Dust from sanding old paint may contain lead, especially in older buildings. Wet sanding or using a vacuum sander reduces dust. For your business, keep a preparation kit stocked and organised. Train your team to follow the same steps every time. Consistency is what turns a small painting business into a reputable contractor. In summary, surface preparation in African climates requires understanding moisture, salts, heat, dust, and substrate diversity. It requires patience and proper materials. But when done right, it reduces callbacks, increases client satisfaction, and allows you to charge premium prices. Your competitors may skip steps. You should not. That is your competitive advantage.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Paints and Coatings for African Markets
lessons.body: In this lesson, we focus on selecting paints and coatings that perform well in African conditions and make business sense. The wrong product choice leads to failures, refunds, and lost reputation. The right choice leads to repeat clients and referrals. Let us start with the basics. Paints are made of four main components: binder, pigment, solvent, and additives. The binder determines the type of paint, such as acrylic, alkyd, or epoxy. The pigment gives colour and opacity. The solvent makes it liquid for application. Additives improve properties like drying time, mould resistance, and UV stability. In Africa, UV stability is critical. The sun is harsh. Cheap paints fade quickly. A client who sees their bright wall turn pale in six months will not call you again. So always check the UV resistance of exterior paints. Look for products with lightfast pigments and UV inhibitors. Acrylic paints are generally better for exterior use because they are flexible and resist UV degradation. Alkyd or oil-based paints are harder and more gloss, but they chalk and fade faster in strong sun. They also yellow. For interiors, acrylics are easier to clean and have low odour. For high-traffic areas like corridors, hospitals, and schools, consider a washable acrylic or a water-based epoxy. Now, let us talk about specific African challenges. Humidity and rain are major factors. In coastal and tropical regions, mould and algae grow on painted surfaces. You need paints that contain fungicides and algaecides. Many manufacturers offer anti-mould paints. Do not assume all exterior paints have these additives. Check the data sheet. Also, in areas with heavy rain, ensure the paint is waterproof, not just water-resistant. Waterproof coatings form a continuous film that repels water. Water-resistant coatings resist some water but can still absorb it over time. For roofs, parapets, and retaining walls, use elastomeric coatings. These are thick, flexible, and bridge small cracks. They are more expensive, but they last longer and prevent water ingress. In dusty regions like the Sahel, paint surfaces get dirty quickly. A gloss or semi-gloss finish is easier to clean than matt. However, gloss shows surface imperfections. So you need to balance aesthetics with practicality. For interior walls in dusty areas, a washable matt or satin finish is a good compromise. For exterior walls, a textured coating can hide imperfections and provide a sacrificial layer that can be cleaned. Now, consider the substrate. Different surfaces need different primers and paints. For new cement, you need an alkali-resistant primer because cement is alkaline. For wood, you need a wood primer that seals the grain and prevents resin bleed. For metal, you need a rust-inhibitive primer. For previously painted surfaces, you need a bonding primer if the old coating is glossy or if you are switching from oil to water-based. In many African markets, you will find a range of local and imported paints. Local paints may be cheaper, but quality varies. Imported paints may be more expensive but consistent. As a business, you should test products before using them on client jobs. Buy a small quantity, apply it to a test panel, and leave it outside for a few months. Check for fading, cracking, peeling, and mould. Build a relationship with reliable suppliers. Ask for technical data sheets and safety data sheets. These give you information on coverage, drying time, thinning, and safety. Do not rely on hearsay. Also, consider the cost per square metre, not just the price per litre. A cheap paint with low coverage may end up costing more because you need more coats. A premium paint with high coverage may be more economical. Calculate the spreading rate. For example, if a paint covers 10 square metres per litre and costs 10 dollars per litre, the cost per square metre is 1 dollar. If a cheaper paint covers 5 square metres per litre and costs 6 dollars per litre, the cost per square metre is 1.20 dollars. The cheaper paint is actually more expensive. Teach your team to do this calculation. It is a simple way to protect your margins. Now, let us discuss speciality coatings. In Africa, there is growing demand for decorative finishes like textured coatings, metallic paints, and faux finishes. These can command higher prices. However, they require skill and practice. Do not offer them until you are confident. Also, consider eco-friendly paints. Some clients, especially in urban areas and in the hospitality industry, prefer low-VOC paints. These are better for indoor air quality and for the environment. They may cost more, but they can be a selling point. Another trend is cool roof coatings. These reflect sunlight and reduce indoor temperatures. In hot African countries, this can lower air conditioning costs. If you can offer this, you open a new market. For your business, create a product portfolio. Have a standard line for everyday jobs and a premium line for high-end clients. Train your staff on the differences. When you quote, explain the options. For example, offer a basic acrylic for a budget-conscious client and a premium elastomeric for a client who wants a long-lasting, waterproof finish. This shows professionalism and helps the client make an informed choice. Finally, storage matters. Paint should be stored in a cool, dry place, away from direct sunlight. In hot climates, paint can spoil. Keep containers sealed. Stir paint before use. Do not use paint that has skin or lumps. For your business, keep inventory levels low but sufficient. Order as needed to avoid old stock. In summary, choosing the right paints and coatings for African markets requires knowledge of UV, humidity, dust, substrate, and budget. It requires testing, calculation, and communication. When you get it right, you deliver value and build a profitable, sustainable painting business.

lessons.title: Application Techniques for Quality and Speed
lessons.body: This lesson is about application techniques that deliver quality and speed, which are the two pillars of a profitable painting business. Quality keeps clients. Speed keeps you competitive. In Africa, where labour is often available but training may be limited, mastering technique is a key differentiator. Let us start with tools. The choice of brush, roller, or sprayer depends on the surface, the paint, and the finish required. For small areas, cutting in, and detailed work, use a brush. A good quality brush holds paint well, lays it off smoothly, and does not shed bristles. In many African markets, you can find brushes made of natural bristles for oil-based paints and synthetic bristles for water-based paints. Do not use natural bristles with water-based paint because they absorb water and become limp. For large flat areas, use a roller. Rollers come in different nap lengths. Short nap for smooth surfaces, medium nap for light texture, and long nap for rough surfaces like stucco or brick. The roller cover material matters too. Synthetic covers work for water-based paints. For oil-based, use natural or synthetic blends. A common mistake is using too little paint. A dry roller leaves a stippled, uneven finish. You need enough paint to fill the nap and transfer it evenly. But too much paint causes drips and runs. The right amount is when the roller glides without sliding and the paint looks wet but not pooling. For large exterior walls, a sprayer can be much faster. Airless sprayers are common. They require skill to avoid overspray and to achieve an even coat. You must mask off windows, doors, and areas not to be painted. Spraying is not always suitable in windy conditions, which are common in many African regions. Also, spraying wastes paint if not managed well. For your business, consider investing in a sprayer if you do a lot of large jobs. It can pay for itself in labour savings. Now, let us talk about preparation of the paint. Stir thoroughly. Do not shake water-based paint vigorously because it creates bubbles. For oil-based, you can shake. Check the thinning instructions. Some paints are ready to use. Others need thinning. Over-thinning reduces coverage and durability. Under-thinning makes the paint hard to apply. Use the correct thinner. For water-based, use clean water. For oil-based, use mineral turpentine or white spirit. Never mix different types of paint. Now, application order. Always start from the top and work down. This allows drips to be caught and spread. For walls, cut in the edges first with a brush, then roll the main area. Work in sections of about one square metre. Maintain a wet edge. If you let the edge dry, you will see lap marks. On a hot day, paint dries fast, so you may need to work in smaller sections or add a retarder. On a humid day, paint dries slowly, so you can work in larger sections but must be careful of sagging. For ceilings, use a roller with an extension pole. Wear goggles to protect your eyes from drips. For trim and doors, use a brush. Apply paint in the direction of the grain for wood. For metal, apply in long strokes. For a smooth finish, lay off the paint with light strokes in one direction. Now, let us discuss coats. Most jobs require a primer and two topcoats. A primer seals the surface, improves adhesion, and blocks stains. Do not skip primer to save money. It will cost you more in the long run. The topcoats provide colour and protection. Allow each coat to dry according to the manufacturer's instructions. Do not rush. If you apply a second coat while the first is still wet, you will get a mess. In dusty environments, cover surfaces that are not being painted. Use drop cloths or plastic sheets. Clean up as you go. A clean site is a professional site. Now, let us talk about speed. Speed comes from organisation and repetition. Set up your tools and materials before you start. Have a plan for the job. Work in a logical sequence. Avoid walking back and forth. Use the right tool for the job. A sprayer is faster for large areas. A roller is faster than a brush for walls. But do not sacrifice quality for speed. A fast job that looks bad will not get you referrals. Train your team in consistent techniques. Have one person cut in while another rolls. This is called pairing. It speeds up the work and improves the finish. For exterior work, consider the sun. Paint on the shady side first. The sun will dry the paint too fast and cause lap marks. Also, avoid painting in the heat of the day. Early morning or late afternoon is better. In the rainy season, watch the weather. Do not paint if rain is expected within the drying time. Now, let us discuss quality control. After each coat, inspect the surface. Look for missed spots, drips, and uneven texture. Fix them before the next coat. Use a light to check for imperfections. At the end of the job, do a final walkthrough with the client. Point out the quality of your work. Explain the care and maintenance. This reduces complaints and builds trust. For your business, keep records. Note the products used, the coverage, the drying times, and any issues. This helps you quote more accurately in the future. It also helps you replicate successful jobs. Finally, think about safety. Painting involves chemicals. Wear gloves, goggles, and a mask when needed. Ensure good ventilation. Do not eat or drink in the work area. Wash hands after work. In Africa, where many painters work informally, safety is often neglected. But a professional business prioritises safety. It protects your workers and reduces liability. In summary, application techniques for quality and speed require the right tools, proper paint preparation, correct order of work, and consistent methods. By mastering these, you can deliver beautiful finishes quickly, satisfy clients, and grow your business.

lessons.title: Estimating, Quoting, and Managing Client Expectations
lessons.body: This lesson is about the business side of painting and decorating: estimating, quoting, and managing client expectations. In Africa, many painters are skilled but struggle to make a profit because they underquote or fail to communicate clearly. This lesson will help you price your work correctly and keep clients happy. First, let us talk about estimating. An estimate is a calculation of the time, materials, and labour required for a job. A quote is a fixed price you offer to the client. To estimate accurately, you need to measure the area to be painted. Measure the length and height of each wall. Multiply to get the square metres. Subtract areas not being painted, like windows and doors. For ceilings, measure the floor area. For trim, measure the linear metres. For textured surfaces, add 20 to 30 percent more paint because the surface area is greater. For porous surfaces, add more primer. Now, calculate the paint needed. Check the spreading rate on the paint container. It is usually given in square metres per litre. Divide the total area by the spreading rate. This gives you the litres per coat. Multiply by the number of coats. Do not forget primer. Add a contingency of 10 percent for waste and touch-ups. Now, calculate labour. How long will the job take? Consider preparation, priming, painting, and cleanup. A common mistake is to underestimate preparation. As we discussed in Lesson 1, preparation can be 60 to 70 percent of the time. If you are unsure, add extra time. It is better to overestimate and finish early than to underestimate and lose money. Labour rates vary across Africa. In some countries, you pay daily wages. In others, you pay per square metre. Know your local market. But do not compete only on price. Compete on quality and reliability. Now, add overheads. Overheads include transport, tools, insurance, and administrative costs. If you have an office, include rent. If you use a vehicle, include fuel and maintenance. Add a profit margin. A typical profit margin in painting is 15 to 30 percent. Do not be afraid to charge for your expertise. A professional job is worth more than a cheap job that fails. Now, let us talk about quoting. A quote should be clear and detailed. It should include the scope of work, the products to be used, the number of coats, the timeline, and the payment terms. It should also state what is not included, such as moving furniture or repairing structural damage. This prevents misunderstandings. For example, if the client has a leaking roof, state that the leak must be fixed before painting. If not, your warranty is void. Present the quote professionally. Use a printed form or a digital document. Include your business name, contact details, and a quote number. This makes you look serious. Now, managing client expectations. This starts before you start the job. Discuss the client's expectations. What colour do they want? What finish? How long will it take? Are there any special requirements? Be honest about what is possible. If the wall is uneven, explain that paint will not fix it. If the old paint is peeling, explain that it must be removed. If the weather is unpredictable, explain that the timeline may change. During the job, keep the client informed. Send progress photos. If there is a delay, communicate early. Do not wait for the client to complain. After the job, do a walkthrough. Show the client the finished work. Explain how to care for the paint. Provide a warranty. A warranty should be in writing. It should state what is covered and what is not. For example, you might warrant the paint for two years against peeling and flaking, provided the client maintains the surface and fixes any water leaks. This protects you and gives the client confidence. Now, let us talk about payments. Never start a job without a deposit. A deposit covers your initial costs for materials and labour. A common arrangement is 50 percent deposit, 40 percent on completion, and 10 percent after a final inspection. Or 30 percent deposit, 40 percent progress payment, and 30 percent on completion. Adjust based on the job size and your cash flow. Always provide a receipt. Keep records. For your business, use a simple accounting system. Track your income and expenses. Know which jobs are profitable and which are not. If you are losing money on a type of job, either raise your prices or stop doing that type of job. Now, let us discuss difficult clients. Some clients will try to negotiate down your price. Some will ask for extra work without paying. Some will complain about everything. Handle these situations professionally. Stick to your quote. If the client wants extra work, provide a variation order with a new price. If the client complains, listen and address the issue. If it is your fault, fix it. If it is not, explain politely. Do not get into arguments. Your reputation is more important than one job. Finally, think about marketing. Your best marketing is a satisfied client. Ask for referrals. Ask for testimonials. Take photos of your work. Use social media and local advertising. In Africa, word of mouth is powerful. A good reputation can bring you more work than any advertisement. In summary, estimating, quoting, and managing client expectations are essential business skills. They ensure you get paid fairly, avoid disputes, and build a sustainable painting business. By mastering these, you can turn your trade into a profitable enterprise.

lessons.title: Health, Safety, and Environmental Responsibility on Site
lessons.body: This lesson covers health, safety, and environmental responsibility on painting and decorating sites in Africa. As a professional business, you have a duty to protect your workers, your clients, and the environment. This is not just a legal requirement in many countries; it is a moral one. It also improves your reputation and reduces costs from accidents and fines. Let us start with personal protective equipment, or PPE. Painting involves chemicals, dust, and physical hazards. The minimum PPE for a painter includes gloves, safety goggles, and a dust mask. For solvent-based paints, you may need a respirator with organic vapour cartridges. For sanding, a dust mask is essential. For working at heights, a safety harness. For handling heavy materials, safety boots. In many African markets, PPE is affordable and available. Do not let your workers work without it. Provide it, train them to use it, and enforce its use. Next, let us talk about chemical safety. Paints, thinners, and cleaners can be harmful if inhaled, swallowed, or contacted with skin. Always read the safety data sheet, or SDS, for each product. The SDS tells you the hazards, first aid measures, and safe handling procedures. Store chemicals in a locked, ventilated area away from food and water. Keep them in their original containers. Never transfer to unlabelled bottles. When mixing, do it in a well-ventilated area. Avoid breathing vapours. If you feel dizzy, move to fresh air. Wash skin contact immediately with soap and water. If paint gets in your eyes, rinse with clean water for 15 minutes and seek medical help. Now, let us discuss fire safety. Many paints and thinners are flammable. Do not smoke near them. Do not use open flames. Keep a fire extinguisher on site. Know how to use it. Store rags soaked in oil-based paint in a sealed metal container because they can spontaneously combust. Dispose of them properly. Now, let us talk about site safety. Painting sites can have hazards like ladders, scaffolding, electrical cords, and wet floors. Keep the site tidy. Remove debris. Secure ladders. Use scaffolding with guardrails. Do not overload electrical sockets. Use residual current devices, or RCDs, to prevent electric shock. If you are working at height, ensure the ladder is on a stable surface and at the correct angle. Do not stand on the top rung. For exterior work, be aware of overhead power lines. Do not use metal ladders near them. Now, let us discuss environmental responsibility. Painting can harm the environment if not managed properly. Paint and thinners should never be poured down drains or onto the ground. They can contaminate water sources. Collect waste in containers and dispose of it at approved facilities. If you cannot find a facility, let the paint dry out and dispose of it as solid waste. Clean brushes in a bucket, not under a running tap. Let the paint solids settle, then dispose of them. Reuse the water if possible. Choose low-VOC paints when you can. They are better for indoor air quality and for the environment. In Africa, where many communities rely on groundwater, protecting water sources is critical. Now, let us talk about worker health. Painting is physically demanding. Workers may suffer from back pain, joint pain, and respiratory issues. Encourage breaks. Provide drinking water. Rotate tasks to avoid repetitive strain. Train workers on safe lifting techniques. If a worker is injured, provide first aid and seek medical attention. Keep a first aid kit on site. For your business, have a safety policy. It should state your commitment to safety, the responsibilities of workers, and the procedures for reporting incidents. Train your team on the policy. Review it regularly. Keep records of training and incidents. This protects you legally and shows clients that you are professional. Now, let us discuss client safety. When working in occupied buildings, protect the client's property. Cover furniture and floors. Keep dust to a minimum. Warn the client about wet paint and strong odours. If the client has allergies or respiratory conditions, use low-odour paints. Schedule work when the area is less used. For exterior work, be careful of falling paint or tools. Use barriers if necessary. Now, let us talk about community responsibility. In many African communities, painting work is visible. Be respectful. Do not make excessive noise early in the morning or late at night. Do not block roads or pathways. Manage waste properly. If you are working in a public space, get permission. Leave the site clean. A clean site reflects well on your business. Finally, let us discuss legal compliance. In many African countries, there are laws and regulations about waste disposal, worker safety, and building codes. Know the laws in your area. If you are unsure, ask a local authority or a professional association. Comply with them. This protects you from fines and lawsuits. It also makes you a responsible business. In summary, health, safety, and environmental responsibility are not optional. They are part of being a professional painter and decorator. By protecting your workers, your clients, and the environment, you build a business that is sustainable, respected, and profitable. This is the mark of a true professional.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Paint Systems, Substrates, and Site Conditions in African Markets

This Practical Reference lesson closes Module 8 by giving you a single, field-ready document you can carry on site. It consolidates the technical data that separates a professional painter-decorator from a casual labourer: how much paint a surface actually needs, how African heat and humidity change drying and adhesion, what substrates are common in your market, and how to price the job so you make money. Every figure below is sourced so you can defend your quotation to a client and your margins to yourself.

Treat this as your bench manual. When a client asks "why does it cost that much?", you open this page. When a foreman asks "how many litres for this wall?", you open this page. When a competitor undercuts you by 40%, you open this page and show the client what a proper system costs â and what skipping steps will cost them in two rainy seasons.

Table 1: Spreading Rates and Coverage by Substrate (African Site Conditions)

These figures are conservative â they assume porous, textured, or previously unpainted surfaces common in African markets. If you quote using the optimistic "smooth surface" numbers on the tin, you will run out of paint and eat the loss. Always measure the wall, then apply the real-world rate below.

Substrate Typical condition Spreading rate (mÂ²/L) Coats required Source
Cement render / plaster New, porous, high alkali 5â7 1 primer + 2 topcoats Dulux / AkzoNobel technical data; adapted for tropical porosity
Cement render / plaster Previously painted, sound 8â10 2 topcoats Dulux / AkzoNobel technical data
Concrete block Unpainted, rough 4â6 1 primer + 2 topcoats PPG / Sigma technical data
Clay brick Unpainted, absorbent 4â5 1 primer + 2 topcoats PPG / Sigma technical data
Wood (softwood) Bare, sanded 10â12 1 primer + 2 topcoats FAO Forestry Paper on wood preservation
Wood (hardwood) Bare, sanded 12â14 1 primer + 2 topcoats FAO Forestry Paper on wood preservation
Metal (ferrous) Bare, rust-free 10â12 1 primer + 2 topcoats ISO 12944 guidance
Metal (ferrous) Rusted, pitted 6â8 1 primer + 2 topcoats ISO 12944 guidance

How to use this in a quote: measure the wall area in mÂ², divide by the spreading rate, multiply by the number of coats, and add 10% waste for brush/roller loss and touch-ups. That is your paint quantity. Multiply by your local supplier price per litre, add labour, transport, consumables, and your margin. Never quote from memory.

Table 2: Drying, Recoating, and Working Time by Climate Zone

African climates are not uniform. The following table uses real meteorological ranges from FAO and WMO data to show how temperature and relative humidity change your working window. These figures assume water-based acrylic paints, which dominate the affordable end of the market. Solvent-based paints behave differently â always check the manufacturer's data sheet.

Climate zone (example cities) Typical temp (Â°C) Typical RH (%) Touch dry Recoat Full cure
Sahel / semi-arid (Dakar, Niamey, Khartoum) 30â42 15â40 20â30 min 2â3 h 5â7 days
Savannah / plateau (Nairobi, Lusaka, Harare) 18â28 40â65 30â45 min 3â4 h 7â10 days
Coastal tropical (Lagos, Mombasa, Dar es Salaam) 26â34 70â90 45â60 min 4â6 h 10â14 days
Equatorial rainforest (Kinshasa, Libreville, Douala) 24â32 80â95 60â90 min 6â8 h 14â21 days
Highland / temperate (Addis Ababa, Kampala, Kigali) 15â25 50â75 40â60 min 4â5 h 7â14 days
Mediterranean (Cape Town, Casablanca, Tunis) 15â30 45â75 30â50 min 3â5 h 7â10 days

Source basis: temperature and humidity ranges from FAO climate data and WMO regional climate summaries; drying and recoat times from AkzoNobel, PPG, and BASF technical data sheets for water-based acrylic systems, adjusted for the humidity ranges shown. Full cure times are indicative and assume good ventilation and no rain.

Business implication: in coastal and equatorial zones, your recoat window can double. That means you cannot paint a whole house in one day. Price your labour for the real number of days, not the number you wish it was. A painter who quotes three days for a coastal job that needs five will lose money and blame the client. A painter who quotes five and delivers five keeps the client and the margin.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICAL AND HEALTH HAZARDS

  • Lead: older buildings in many African cities may still have lead-based paint. Sanding or burning it releases toxic dust and fumes. WHO identifies lead exposure as a major cause of irreversible neurological damage in children. Test before you strip. Never dry-sand suspected lead paint.
  • Solvents: solvent-based paints and thinners release volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Work only in ventilated spaces. Wear a respirator rated for organic vapours â a dust mask is not enough.
  • Skin contact: wet cement, primers, and solvents cause chemical burns and dermatitis. Wear gloves, long sleeves, and eye protection.
  • Heat stress: in Sahel and savannah conditions, painters can suffer heat exhaustion within hours. Schedule heavy work for early morning, provide water and shade, and rotate tasks.
  • Disposal: never pour paint or solvent down drains or onto open ground. Collect residues and dispose through licensed waste handlers. WHO and UNEP both flag improper paint disposal as a water-contamination risk.
  • Spraying: spray application in enclosed spaces requires forced ventilation and full respiratory protection. Isocyanates in some two-pack systems can cause severe asthma.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Measure before you quote. Wall area in mÂ², number of coats, spreading rate from Table 1, plus 10% waste. No guessing.
  2. Identify the substrate. Cement, block, brick, wood, or metal â each needs a different primer and system.
  3. Check the climate zone. Use Table 2 to set realistic recoat and cure times. Coastal and equatorial jobs take longer.
  4. Test for lead and damp. On buildings older than 1980, assume lead until tested. On any wall, check for rising damp and soluble salts before painting.
  5. Prepare properly. Clean, sand, fill, and prime. Skipping primer on new cement is the most common cause of peeling in African markets.
  6. Protect yourself and your team. Gloves, eye protection, respirator for solvents, water and shade for heat. No exceptions.
  7. Price for the real job. Include paint, labour, transport, consumables, waste disposal, and margin. A cheap quote is a future dispute.
  8. Hand over with documentation. Give the client the product data sheets, the colour codes, and a simple maintenance schedule. This is how you get the next job.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Forestry Publications on Wood Preservation and Tropical Building Materials â free technical papers on protecting timber and masonry in humid climates.
  • WHO â Lead Poisoning and Health Fact Sheet â essential reading before any renovation of older buildings.
  • UNEP â Chemicals and Waste Programme â guidance on safe disposal of paints, solvents, and site waste.
  • ISO 12944 â Corrosion Protection of Steel Structures by Protective Paint Systems â the international standard for metal painting systems.
  • ILO â Occupational Safety and Health â free resources on construction-site health and safety, including heat stress and chemical exposure.

quiz.q: Which type of paint is most suitable for a high-traffic hallway wall that needs to be washable?
options: A) Emulsion with a matt finish
B) Emulsion with a silk finish
C) Distemper
D) Limewash
quiz.explanation: Silk emulsion forms a tougher, more washable film than matt, making it suitable for high-traffic areas.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a primer when painting bare timber?
options: A) To add colour
B) To seal knots and provide a key for subsequent coats
C) To create a high-gloss finish
D) To act as a final topcoat
quiz.explanation: Primer seals the timber, blocks knots and creates a surface that topcoats can bond to.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for cutting in a neat edge between a wall and a ceiling?
options: A) A roller with a long pile sleeve
B) A paint pad
C) A 2 inch angled sash brush
D) A spray gun
quiz.explanation: An angled sash brush gives the control needed for cutting in clean edges along ceilings and trim.

quiz.q: What does the term cutting in mean in painting and decorating?
options: A) Mixing two colours together
B) Removing old paint with a scraper
C) Applying a second coat before the first is dry
D) Painting a neat edge along a boundary before rolling the main area
quiz.explanation: Cutting in is painting a controlled edge along ceilings, corners and trim so the larger area can be rolled up to it.

quiz.q: Which abrasive grade is most suitable for lightly keying a previously painted gloss surface before recoating?
options: A) Fine grade such as 180 to 240 grit
B) Very coarse grade such as 40 grit
C) Medium grade such as 80 grit
D) Extra coarse grade such as 24 grit
quiz.explanation: A fine abrasive keys the gloss surface without scratching through the existing coating.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for preparing a new plaster wall before painting?
options: A) Apply topcoat, then primer, then filler
B) Allow to dry, seal with mist coat, fill imperfections, then apply finish coats
C) Fill first, then wash with solvent, then apply gloss
D) Apply two gloss coats directly to bare plaster
quiz.explanation: New plaster must dry fully, be sealed with a mist coat, have imperfections filled and sanded, then receive finish coats.

quiz.q: Which safety precaution is most important when using solvent-based paint in an enclosed room?
options: A) Wearing a dust mask only
B) Keeping the door closed to contain odours
C) Ensuring good ventilation and wearing suitable respiratory protection
D) Using water to dilute the paint
quiz.explanation: Solvent-based paints release harmful vapours, so ventilation and correct respiratory protection are essential.

quiz.q: Why should a roller sleeve be matched to the type of paint being used?
options: A) To change the colour of the paint
B) To make the paint dry faster
C) To reduce the number of coats required
D) To control the finish and avoid shedding or poor coverage
quiz.explanation: The correct sleeve material and pile length give proper pickup and release, ensuring a good finish without shedding or patchiness.
